explain.say: Imagine hearing that, on a certain day, the taps in your whole city would be switched off, and you would queue for water with a bucket. In 2018 that nearly happened in Cape Town, a South African city of more than 4 million people. Look at the board: here is how it happened.

explain.say: It started in 2015, when the winter rains that fill Cape Town’s dams began to fail. Three dry winters in a row! Meanwhile the city had grown and was using more water. Can you see the problem building up?

explain.say: By January 2018 the dams were so low that the city warned of Day Zero: the day most taps would be turned off, maybe in April. People would collect 25 litres each a day from about 200 collection points. How would your family manage?

explain.say: So everyone was asked to use just 50 litres a day. That is less than one bathtub, for drinking, cooking, washing and flushing, for a whole day! People took two-minute showers and flushed toilets with leftover washing water. Could you do it?

faq.a: Day Zero was the day Cape Town’s dams would fall to 13.5 percent full, when most taps would be turned off and people would collect 25 litres each a day from collection points. Thanks to water saving and rain, it never came.
asks: Did Cape Town run out of water?
What was Day Zero in Cape Town?

faq.q: Why did Cape Town run short of water?
faq.a: From 2015 to 2018 the city had its worst drought in about a century, with three very dry winters. Its water comes mostly from rain-fed dams, and its population had grown fast.
asks: What caused the Cape Town drought?

faq.q: How much is 50 litres of water?
faq.a: About five large buckets, less than a full bathtub. Many people in rich countries use well over 100 litres each a day at home.
asks: How much water does a person use each day?

faq.q: How can cities avoid running out of water?
faq.a: By fixing leaks, saving water, recycling used water, pumping groundwater carefully, collecting rainwater and, by the sea, desalination, which means removing salt from seawater.

Water scarcity means there is not enough clean water for everyone’s needs. It can happen because there is little water, or because there is no money for pipes and treatment. About 2 billion people lack safe drinking water at home.
asks: How many people lack clean water?

facts: Day Zero was the day Cape Town's dams would fall to 13.5%, when most taps would be turned off.
From February 2018 Cape Town residents were asked to use no more than 50 litres of water per person per day.
Cape Town roughly halved its water use between 2015 and 2018.
